Issued at 235 PM CDT Tue Sep 22 2026

A somewhat chaotic flow pattern is found over the northern 
Plains this afternoon as a developing ridge to the west of the 
forecast butts up against an exiting upper level low exiting 
into the Great Lakes Region. Increasingly cloudy skies are 
expected through the afternoon and evening as moisture returns 
from the Gulf increase across the state. Highs today will thus 
be warmest in the upper 60s to lower 70s across the northwest 
and north central where partly cloudy to mostly clear skies 
linger the longest, while the southwest and south central will 
only peak into the lower to mid 60s. Breezy south to 
southeasterly winds, with sustained speeds up to around 25 MPH 
and gusts up to 35 MPH, will be found as a modest pressure 
gradient is draped across the northern Plains and will linger 
overnight into early Wednesday. Otherwise, the increasing cloud 
cover and persistant southerly surface flow are expected to keep
low temperatures tonight mainly in the mid 40s to lower 50s. 

Upper level flow over the northern Plains is then expected to 
consolidate and turn increasingly southwesterly late tonight 
into early Wednesday as a shortwave perturbation passes through 
the area. Along with the increasing moisture across the area, 
this wave will promote medium to high (50 to 80 percent) chances
for showers across western and central North Dakota starting 
Wednesday morning, with isolated thunderstorms also possible (20
to 30 percent) Wednesday afternoon and evening. While the 
initial convective environment is expected to be fairly tame, 
with MUCAPE values peaking only around 500-750 J/KG above the 
prevailing cloud layer and cooler surface temperatures, there is
some potential for an isolated stronger storm over the 
southwest into the south central late Wednesday afternoon into 
Wednesday evening as a weak cold front/surface trough is pulled 
across the area. The overall potential for hazards remains low, 
with sub severe winds and maybe some small expected with any 
stronger storm that does develop. Storm total rain through late 
Wednesday are anticipated to be light, with amounts generally 
from around 0.10" across the west up to around 0.25" to 0.75" 
central. While the current calibrated NBM chance to exceed 1.00"
is low through this period, around 15 to 35 percent across 
portions of the northern James River Valley, high model PWATs 
around 1.25" indicate that locally higher totals can be 
anticipated where and when thunderstorms develop. Otherwise, for
Wednesday, highs in the 60s to lower 70s can be anticipated as 
prevailing clouds and showers limit diurnal heating potential. 

For the end of the workweek, the amplification of a transient 
upper level ridge across the northern Plains on Thursday will 
promote clearing skies, dry weather, and warmer temperatures in 
the lower 70s and 80s. Then, heading into Friday, low to medium 
chances (30 to 50 percent) for showers will pass across much of 
western and central North Dakota as another shortwave 
perturbation ejects off of the western Rockies and passes north 
across the forecast area. The overall potential for 
thunderstorms appears to be fairly limited through the day on 
Friday, with ensemble members advertising the better convective 
environment further to the south and east of the forecast area. 
While it wouldn't be overly surprising to see a rumble of 
thunder or two in the far southern James River Valley, mainly 
showers can be anticipated at this time. Overall QPF is also 
expected to be fairly limited, with the calibrated NBM 5.0 
probability for more than 0.25" of rain fairly low (20 to 40 
percent). Otherwise for Friday, the increased cloud cover 
associated with the showers will help put a damper on the above 
normal temperatures previously forecast in earlier cycles, with 
highs now expected to range in the mid 60s to mid 70s. 

Looking ahead, the weekend is going to be characterized the 
passage of a strong pacific trough/closed low across the 
Canadian Prairies. Mainly dry and warm (highs in the 60s and 
70s) conditions are expected as flow over the northern Plains 
turns southwesterly on the leading edge of the trough. The 
prevailing southeasterly winds over turn northwesterly on 
Saturday as a cold front is lofted through the area, though poor
saturation throughout the vertical profile will limit overall 
chances for precipitation. The ensemble continues to delay the 
onset precipitation over the Dakotas compared to previous 
forecast cycles, due to the slightly slower evolution of this 
trough. There is fairly strong agreement between ensemble 
members for showers some time Monday through the early workweek,
though there is a hint in some clusters (approx 30 percent of 
members) of a more divergent flow pattern over the northern 
Plains. In this particular scenario, much of the forecast area 
would struggle to see much measurable precpitation.
